title: The Fed holds at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent and slows Treasury runoff
summary: The FOMC left the federal funds target range unchanged, said uncertainty around the outlook had increased, and cut the monthly cap on Treasury runoff from $25 billion to $5 billion starting in April. Governor Waller dissented on the runoff change only.

source.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
source.title: Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
source.published_as_stated: March 19, 2025 · For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT
source.timezone_note: EDT is Eastern Daylight Time, UTC−04:00, so the release time is 18:00 UTC.
source.reference_period: Not a data release: the statement announces the Committee's decision of March 19, 2025.

overview: The statement makes two decisions. The policy rate is unchanged: the target range for the federal funds rate stays at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. The balance sheet keeps shrinking, but more slowly: beginning in April, the monthly cap on Treasury securities allowed to run off falls from $25 billion to $5 billion, while the $35 billion cap on agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities stays.

Compared with the January 29, 2025 statement, the economic assessment is word for word the same: activity 'has continued to expand at a solid pace', the unemployment rate 'has stabilized at a low level', and inflation 'remains somewhat elevated'. Two sentences changed. January's judgment that the risks to the Committee's goals were 'roughly in balance' is gone, and 'The economic outlook is uncertain' became 'Uncertainty around the economic outlook has increased.'

The vote changed too. In January the decision was unanimous; in March Governor Waller voted against, supporting no change to the rate but preferring to continue the current pace of decline in securities holdings. The disagreement is about runoff, not about rates.

key_facts.basis: Beginning in April 2025; the most that can run off in a month

Uncertainty

key_facts.basis: Replaces January's 'The economic outlook is uncertain'

channels.title: Expected policy path (shorter maturities)
channels.source_fact: The range is unchanged, and the guidance on further adjustments ('carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks') is the same as in January.
channels.interpretation: Two-year yields mostly reflect the expected path of the policy rate. An unchanged rate with unchanged guidance adds little to that path by itself. Any effect through this channel would have to come from how investors read the deleted 'roughly in balance' judgment and the stronger uncertainty sentence, for instance as a higher chance of future cuts, which would tend to lower shorter yields. The statement does not say which way the Committee leans.

channels.title: Runoff and Treasury supply (longer maturities)
channels.source_fact: From April, at most $5 billion of Treasury holdings a month may run off instead of $25 billion; the agency cap is unchanged.
channels.interpretation: Maturing Treasuries above the cap are rolled over by the Federal Reserve, so a lower cap leaves less for private investors to refinance. If investors see that as less duration for the private market to absorb, term premiums and longer yields could be somewhat lower than otherwise. The $20 billion cut is a maximum: how much supply actually changes depends on monthly maturities and on Treasury's financing choices, which the statement does not give.

channels.title: Stated uncertainty (either direction)
channels.source_fact: 'Uncertainty around the economic outlook has increased.' The statement attaches no policy commitment to it.
channels.interpretation: Greater uncertainty can pull yields both ways: toward lower front-end yields if it raises the perceived chance of cuts, or toward higher longer yields if investors demand more compensation for holding duration. Without other evidence the sign of this channel is unknown, and treating it as directional would be a guess.

competing_explanations.title: Runoff as plumbing, not stance
competing_explanations.detail: The statement gives no reason for slowing runoff. If investors read it as a technical step about reserves or money-market conditions rather than a signal about the policy stance, it would leave rate expectations unchanged, and a small expected supply change could be swamped by Treasury's own issuance.

competing_explanations.title: Other communications around the decision
competing_explanations.detail: Federal Reserve communications beyond this statement, which this case does not use, could have moved rate expectations more than the statement did, in either direction, overriding the channels above.

competing_explanations.title: Inflation still 'somewhat elevated'
competing_explanations.detail: The same text keeps inflation 'somewhat elevated' and reaffirms the 2 percent objective. A reader weighting that sentence would see no new reason to expect earlier cuts, offsetting a dovish reading of the uncertainty language.

assumptions: Treasury yields respond to changes in the expected policy path and in the expected net supply of duration, not only to the current policy rate.
A lower redemption cap reduces the Treasury supply that private investors must absorb, rather than being offset by changes in Treasury's issuance.
Investors read the statement's wording changes against January's text, as this case does.
missing_information: A sourced, contemporaneous measure of what investors expected for the rate and for runoff. Without it this case cannot say whether either decision was a surprise.
The Federal Reserve's monthly Treasury maturities, which determine how far the old and new caps actually bind.
Other materials around the decision, including the Implementation Note linked from the release and the minutes published later, which may explain the reasoning; none is used.
Treasury's financing plans for the following quarters, which shape how any change in Federal Reserve runoff reaches private holdings.
weakening_observations: Evidence that the runoff slowdown was widely anticipated before March 19, for example from earlier Federal Reserve communications, would make this release a weak carrier of the supply channel.
If the Federal Reserve's monthly Treasury maturities were often below $25 billion, the old cap did not bind and the effective change is smaller than $20 billion a month.
If later Federal Reserve communications attributed the change mainly to money-market technicalities, the term-premium reading would weaken.
If longer yields showed no movement separable from other news around the release, the supply channel would have no support in this event.

critique.title: Two decisions in one release
critique.detail: A rate decision (no change) and a runoff decision (a change) arrive together, and their channels work at different maturities, so any single-yield reading of this event is confounded. A cleaner analysis would state separate implications for shorter and longer maturities, and would need the day's other communications to isolate the rate-path part.

critique.title: A cap is not a quantity
critique.detail: It is tempting to treat '$20 billion a month less runoff' as the supply change. It is an upper bound. Without the monthly maturity schedule the effective change could be much smaller, so the supply channel's size is unknown here, and this case deliberately gives no magnitude.

critique.title: Wording changes are easy to over-read
critique.detail: The deleted 'roughly in balance' sentence and the stronger uncertainty sentence are real changes, but the statement attaches no policy commitment to them. Reading them as a dovish signal is an interpretation the text alone does not support. This case leaves their sign open, which also limits what it can explain.

critique.title: Chosen and written after the fact
critique.detail: This statement is the second of four consecutive 2025 FOMC statements in the library, included by that rule rather than for any outcome, and analysed in October 2026 by an AI assistant that may know how 2025 unfolded. The text avoids later events, but hindsight could still shape which channels look important. Nothing here was frozen before publication, so it carries no evidence about forecasting.

source_notes.title: Text used
source_notes.detail: The statement as published on the release page, which shows 'Last Update: March 19, 2025'. A PDF version and an Implementation Note are linked from the page and are not used.

source_notes.title: Comparison text
source_notes.detail: Wording changes are measured against the January 29, 2025 FOMC statement, released at 2:00 p.m. EST.

source_notes.title: No revisions apply
source_notes.detail: A policy statement is not a statistical estimate and is not revised. Later Federal Reserve communications may explain or reinterpret it; none is used here.
